newsitem.title: UK: Former UK Chancellor praises Brown's reforms.
newsitem.headline: Former UK Chancellor praises Brown's reforms.

text.p: Former Conservative Chancellor of the Exchequer Norman Lamont on Tuesday congratulated Gordon Brown, the new Labour finance minister, on his radical reforms of British monetary policy.

"I'm delighted Gordon Brown has decided to give the Bank full operational independence," Lamont told Reuters. "This change is right and should have been made by Conservative governments. Gordon Brown deserves credit for this bold move."

In his first act as finance minister on Tuesday, Brown stunned financial markets by announcing that the Bank of England would be allowed to set interest rates. He also raised interest rates to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent.

From next month, a new monetary policy committee will set interest rates to meet an inflation target laid down by the government. Previously, the Chancellor alone set interest rates after taking advice from the Bank of England.
Lamont's comments contrasted with the reaction of Kenneth Clarke, his successor as Chancellor and Brown's immediate predecessor.

Clarke described the decision as "unwise and precipitate" and said Brown would come to regret it. "What you are going to see is, undoubtedly, tighter monetary policy than you might otherwise have," he told BBC Radio.
The new Labour chancellor said he wanted to remove "the suspicion that short-term party-political considerations are influencing the setting of interest rates."

"Sound money is the people's right. Interest rate changes should not be in the hands of politicians, subject to all sorts of political pressures," he said, adding that the reforms would enhance the credibility of economic policy.
Lamont was Chancellor from 1990 until 1993, when he paid the price for Britain's ignominious exit from the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992 and lost his Cabinet post.
He was one of many leading Conservatives who lost their parliamentary seats in last week's Labour election landslide.
Lamont started the process of opening up the monetary policy structure, instituting monthly monetary meetings and publishing the minutes of those meetings.

Lamont was also dismissive of Kenneth Clarke's assertion on Tuesday that subsequent low inflation had vindicated Clarke's decision to reject the Bank of England's calls for higher interest rates last year. "He was lucky," Lamont said scathingly.
